source_text:
CHAPTER LV.

        “Ritorna a tua scienza
  Che vuol, quanto la cosa e più perfetta
  Più senta il bene, e cosi la doglienza.”
                                         —DANTE.


When Deronda met Gwendolen and Grandcourt on the staircase, his mind
was seriously preoccupied. He had just been summoned to the second
interview with his mother.

In two hours after his parting from her he knew that the Princess
Halm-Eberstein had left the hotel, and so far as the purpose of his
journey to Genoa was concerned, he might himself have set off on his
way to Mainz, to deliver the letter from Joseph Kalonymos, and get
possession of the family chest. But mixed mental conditions, which did
not resolve themselves into definite reasons, hindered him from
departure. Long after the farewell he was kept passive by a weight of
retrospective feeling. He lived again, with the new keenness of emotive
memory, through the exciting scenes which seemed past only in the sense
of preparation for their actual presence in his soul. He allowed
himself in his solitude to sob, with perhaps more than a woman’s
acuteness of compassion, over that woman’s life so near to his, and yet
so remote. He beheld the world changed for him by the certitude of ties
that altered the poise of hopes and fears, and gave him a new sense of
fellowship, as if under cover of the night he had joined the wrong band
of wanderers, and found with the rise of morning that the tents of his
kindred were grouped far off. He had a quivering imaginative sense of
close relation to the grandfather who had been animated by strong
impulses and beloved thoughts, which were now perhaps being roused from
their slumber within himself. And through all this passionate
meditation Mordecai and Mirah were always present, as beings who
clasped hands with him in sympathetic silence.

Of such quick, responsive fibre was Deronda made, under that mantle of
self-controlled reserve into which early experience had thrown so much
of his young strength.

When the persistent ringing of a bell as a signal reminded him of the
hour he thought of looking into _Bradshaw_, and making the brief
necessary preparations for starting by the next train—thought of it,
but made no movement in consequence. Wishes went to Mainz and what he
was to get possession of there—to London and the beings there who made
the strongest attachments of his life; but there were other wishes that
clung in these moments to Genoa, and they kept him where he was by that
force which urges us to linger over an interview that carries a
presentiment of final farewell or of overshadowing sorrow. Deronda did
not formally say, “I will stay over to-night, because it is Friday, and
I should like to go to the evening service at the synagogue where they
must all have gone; and besides, I may see the Grandcourts again.” But
simply, instead of packing and ringing for his bill, he sat doing
nothing at all, while his mind went to the synagogue and saw faces
there probably little different from those of his grandfather’s time,
and heard the Spanish-Hebrew liturgy which had lasted through the
seasons of wandering generations like a plant with wandering seed, that
gives the far-off lands a kinship to the exile’s home—while, also, his
mind went toward Gwendolen, with anxious remembrance of what had been,
and with a half-admitted impression that it would be hardness in him
willingly to go away at once without making some effort, in spite of
Grandcourt’s probable dislike, to manifest the continuance of his
sympathy with her since their abrupt parting.

In this state of mind he deferred departure, ate his dinner without
sense of flavor, rose from it quickly to find the synagogue, and in
passing the porter asked if Mr. and Mrs. Grandcourt were still in the
hotel, and what was the number of their apartment. The porter gave him
the number, but added that they were gone out boating. That information
had somehow power enough over Deronda to divide his thoughts with the
memories wakened among the sparse _talithim_ and keen dark faces of
worshippers whose way of taking awful prayers and invocations with the
easy familiarity which might be called Hebrew dyed Italian, made him
reflect that his grandfather, according to the Princess’s hints of his
character, must have been almost as exceptional a Jew as Mordecai. But
were not men of ardent zeal and far-reaching hope everywhere
exceptional? the men who had the visions which, as Mordecai said, were
the creators and feeders of the world—moulding and feeding the more
passive life which without them would dwindle and shrivel into the
narrow tenacity of insects, unshaken by thoughts beyond the reach of
their antennae. Something of a mournful impatience perhaps added itself
to the solicitude about Gwendolen (a solicitude that had room to grow
in his present release from immediate cares) as an incitement to hasten
from the synagogue and choose to take his evening walk toward the quay,
always a favorite haunt with him, and just now attractive with the
possibility that he might be in time to see the Grandcourts come in
from their boating. In this case, he resolved that he would advance to
greet them deliberately, and ignore any grounds that the husband might
have for wishing him elsewhere.

The sun had set behind a bank of cloud, and only a faint yellow light
was giving its farewell kisses to the waves, which were agitated by an
active breeze. Deronda, sauntering slowly within sight of what took
place on the strand, observed the groups there concentrating their
attention on a sailing-boat which was advancing swiftly landward, being
rowed by two men. Amidst the clamorous talk in various languages,
Deronda held it the surer means of getting information not to ask
questions, but to elbow his way to the foreground and be an
unobstructed witness of what was occurring. Telescopes were being used,
and loud statements made that the boat held somebody who had been
drowned. One said it was the _milord_ who had gone out in a sailing
boat; another maintained that the prostrate figure he discerned was
_miladi_; a Frenchman who had no glass would rather say that it was
_milord_ who had probably taken his wife out to drown her, according to
the national practice—a remark which an English skipper immediately
commented on in our native idiom (as nonsense which—had undergone a
mining operation), and further dismissed by the decision that the
reclining figure was a woman. For Deronda, terribly excited by
fluctuating fears, the strokes of the oars as he watched them were
divided by swift visions of events, possible and impossible, which
might have brought about this issue, or this broken-off fragment of an
issue, with a worse half undisclosed—if this woman apparently snatched
from the waters were really Mrs. Grandcourt.

But soon there was no longer any doubt: the boat was being pulled to
land, and he saw Gwendolen half raising herself on her hands, by her
own effort, under her heavy covering of tarpaulin and pea-jackets—pale
as one of the sheeted dead, shivering, with wet hair streaming, a wild
amazed consciousness in her eyes, as if she had waked up in a world
where some judgment was impending, and the beings she saw around were
coming to seize her. The first rower who jumped to land was also wet
through, and ran off; the sailors, close about the boat, hindered
Deronda from advancing, and he could only look on while Gwendolen gave
scared glances, and seemed to shrink with terror as she was carefully,
tenderly helped out, and led on by the strong arms of those rough,
bronzed men, her wet clothes clinging about her limbs, and adding to
the impediment of her weakness. Suddenly her wandering eyes fell on
Deronda, standing before her, and immediately, as if she had been
expecting him and looking for him, she tried to stretch out her arms,
which were held back by her supporters, saying, in a muffled voice,

“It is come, it is come! He is dead!”

“Hush, hush!” said Deronda, in a tone of authority; “quiet yourself.”
Then to the men who were assisting her, “I am a connection of this
lady’s husband. If you will get her on to the _Italia_ as quickly as
possible, I will undertake everything else.”

He stayed behind to hear from the remaining boatman that her husband
had gone down irrecoverably, and that his boat was left floating empty.
He and his comrade had heard a cry, had come up in time to see the lady
jump in after her husband, and had got her out fast enough to save her
from much damage.

After this, Deronda hastened to the hotel to assure himself that the
best medical help would be provided; and being satisfied on this point,
he telegraphed the event to Sir Hugo, begging him to come forthwith,
and also to Mr. Gascoigne, whose address at the rectory made his
nearest known way of getting the information to Gwendolen’s mother.
Certain words of Gwendolen’s in the past had come back to him with the
effectiveness of an inspiration: in moments of agitated confession she
had spoken of her mother’s presence, as a possible help, if she could
have had it.

"The return to your knowledge,
Which seeks how much the thing is more perfect,
More feels the good, and thus the pain."
—Dante.

When Daniel Deronda encountered Gwendolen and Grandcourt upon the stairs, his heart was a storm-tossed sea, utterly preoccupied. Just minutes prior, he had been summoned for a second, harrowing interview with his mother. Now, standing amidst the bustle of the hotel, he felt a strange paralysis. Two hours after leaving her, the Princess Halm-Eberstein had departed, leaving the path clear for Deronda to journey to Mainz, to deliver Joseph Kalonymos's letter and claim the family chest. Yet, a heavy, indeterminate weight anchored him to Genoa. It was not logic, nor duty, but a retrospective grief that held him fast. In the solitude of his own mind, he relived the scene with a fresh, piercing acuity, weeping silently over a life so intimately connected to his own destiny, yet so tragically distant. He felt the world shift beneath his feet; the certitude of ties binding him to a lineage of wanderers altered the balance of his hopes and fears. Under the cover of night, he realized he had wandered in the wrong company, only to find, as dawn approached, that his kindred pitched their tents far away. A quivering imagination stirred within him, sensing a close bond with a grandfather whose strong impulses and deep loves were perhaps waking from a long slumber inside his own soul. Through this passionate meditation, Mordecai and Mirah stood ever present, clasping hands with him in a silent, sympathetic unity.

Such was the fiber of Deronda, quick and responsive, draped beneath a mantle of self-controlled reserve forged by early hardship.

A persistent bell signaled the hour, urging him to consult Bradshaw and prepare for the next train to Mainz. He thought of it, then thought of London, of the beings there who formed the strongest attachments of his life. But other wishes clung to Genoa, rooted in a force that makes us linger over interviews carrying the shadow of final farewells. He did not consciously decide to wait until Friday evening to attend the synagogue service, hoping to see the Grandcourts again. Instead, simply, he sat doing nothing, refusing to pack or ring for his bill. His mind drifted to the synagogue, imagining the faces there—perhaps unchanged from his grandfather's time—and hearing the Spanish-Hebrew liturgy. It sounded like a plant with wandering seeds, spreading across seasons and exiles, weaving a kinship between far-off lands and the homes of the displaced. Simultaneously, his thoughts turned to Gwendolen, haunted by anxious memories of what had passed. There lingered a half-admitted fear that it would be cruel, a form of hardness, to leave immediately without making some effort, despite Grandcourt's likely disapproval, to show his continued sympathy following their abrupt separation.

Thus, he deferred his departure. Dinner tasted of ash, and he rose quickly, asking the porter if Mr. and Mrs. Grandcourt remained in the hotel and for their apartment number. The porter supplied the number but added, with a casual shrug, that they had gone out boating. This single piece of news possessed a power sufficient to split Deronda's focus, dividing it with the memories awakened among the sparse *talithim* and the keen, dark faces of worshippers. Their ease in handling awful prayers and invocations, with a familiarity that seemed like Hebrew dyed Italian, struck him deeply. He reflected that his grandfather, according to the Princess's hints, must have been nearly as exceptional a Jew as Mordecai himself. Were not men of ardent zeal and far-reaching hope everywhere exceptional? Those who hold visions, as Mordecai described, are the creators and feeders of the world, molding the passive lives that would otherwise wither into the narrow tenacity of insects, unshaken by thoughts beyond the reach of their antennae. A mournful impatience mingled with his growing solicitude for Gwendolen, urging him to hasten from the synagogue. He chose an evening walk toward the quay, a favorite haunt, drawn by the possibility that he might catch the Grandcourts returning from their boating trip. If so, he resolved to approach them deliberately, ignoring any grounds Grandcourt might have for wishing him elsewhere.

The sun had dipped behind a bank of clouds, casting only a faint, dying yellow light upon the waves, which churned under an active breeze. Deronda sauntered slowly within sight of the strand, observing the groups concentrating their attention on a sailing-boat approaching swiftly toward land, rowed by two men. Amidst the clamorous chatter in various tongues, Deronda suppressed questions, pushing his way to the foreground to become an unobstructed witness. Telescopes were raised, and loud speculations erupted. "It is the *milord* who has drowned!" one cried. Another insisted the prostrate figure seen below decks was *miladi*. A Frenchman, lacking a glass, ventured that it was *milord*, perhaps taking his wife out to drown her, a notion echoing a certain national practice. An English skipper retorted in his native idiom, dismissing the idea as nonsense that had "undergone a mining operation," finally deciding the reclining figure was indeed a woman. For Deronda, terribly excited by fluctuating terrors, the rhythm of the oars was shattered by swift visions of events, both possible and impossible, leading to this tragic conclusion—or a broken fragment thereof, with a worse half concealed. Could the woman snatched from the waters truly be Mrs. Grandcourt?

Soon, however, doubt vanished. The boat was pulled to shore. Deronda saw Gwendolen, half-raising herself on her hands by sheer effort, encased in a heavy covering of tarpaulins and pea-jackets. She was pale as one of the sheeted dead, shivering, with wet hair streaming down her face. Her eyes held a wild, amazed consciousness, as if she had woken in a world where judgment hung suspended, and the beings surrounding her were coming to seize her. The first rower who leaped onto the sand was soaked through and ran off. The sailors crowded around the boat, blocking Deronda's advance. He could only watch as Gwendolen cast scared glances, shrinking with terror as she was carefully, tenderly lifted out and led away by the strong, bronzed arms of the rough men. Her wet clothes clung to her limbs, adding to the impediment of her weakness. Suddenly, her wandering eyes fell upon Deronda, standing before her. Immediately, as if she had been expecting him, searching for him, she tried to stretch out her arms, though they were held back by her supporters. In a muffled voice, she whispered, "It is come, it is come! He is dead!"

"Hush, hush!" Deronda commanded, his tone authoritative yet gentle. "Quiet yourself." Turning to the men assisting her, he declared, "I am a connection of this lady's husband. If you will get her aboard the *Italia* as quickly as possible, I will undertake everything else."

He remained to learn from the remaining boatman that her husband had gone down irrecoverably, his boat left floating empty in the water. They, along with their companion, had heard a cry and arrived just in time to see the lady jump in after her husband, saving her from terrible damage.

Afterward, Deronda hastened to the hotel to ensure the best medical aid was provided. Once satisfied on this point, he telegraphed the event to Sir Hugo, begging him to arrive forthwith, and also to Mr. Gascoigne, whose residence at the rectory offered the nearest known route to inform Gwendolen's mother. The sun had dipped behind a bank of clouds, casting only a faint, dying yellow light upon the waves, which churned under an active breeze. Deronda sauntered slowly within sight of the strand, observing the groups concentrating their attention on a sailing-boat approaching swiftly toward land, rowed by two men. Amidst the clamorous chatter in various tongues, Deronda suppressed questions, pushing his way to the foreground to become an unobstructed witness. Telescopes were raised, and loud speculations erupted. "It is the *milord* who has drowned!" one cried. Another insisted the prostrate figure seen below decks was *miladi*. A Frenchman, lacking a glass, ventured that it was *milord*, perhaps taking his wife out to drown her, a notion echoing a certain national practice. An English skipper retorted in his native idiom, dismissing the idea as nonsense that had "undergone a mining operation," finally deciding the reclining figure was indeed a woman. For Deronda, terribly excited by fluctuating terrors, the rhythm of the oars was shattered by swift visions of events, both possible and impossible, leading to this tragic conclusion—or a broken fragment thereof, with a worse half concealed. Could the woman snatched from the waters truly be Mrs. Grandcourt?

Soon, however, doubt vanished. The boat was pulled to shore. Deronda saw Gwendolen, half-raising herself on her hands by sheer effort, encased in a heavy covering of tarpaulins and pea-jackets. She was pale as one of the sheeted dead, shivering, with wet hair streaming down her face. Her eyes held a wild, amazed consciousness, as if she had woken in a world where judgment hung suspended, and the beings surrounding her were coming to seize her. The first rower who leaped onto the sand was soaked through and ran off. The sailors crowded around the boat, blocking Deronda's advance. He could only watch as Gwendolen cast scared glances, shrinking with terror as she was carefully, tenderly lifted out and led away by the strong, bronzed arms of the rough men. Her wet clothes clung to her limbs, adding to the impediment of her weakness. Suddenly, her wandering eyes fell upon Deronda, standing before her. Immediately, as if she had been expecting him, searching for him, she tried to stretch out her arms, though they were held back by her supporters. In a muffled voice, she whispered, "It is come, it is come! He is dead!"

"Hush, hush!" Deronda commanded, his tone authoritative yet gentle. "Quiet yourself." Turning to the men assisting her, he declared, "I am a connection of this lady's husband. If you will get her aboard the *Italia* as quickly as possible, I will undertake everything else."

He remained to learn from the remaining boatman that her husband had gone down irrecoverably, his boat left floating empty in the water. They, along with their companion, had heard a cry and arrived just in time to see the lady jump in after her husband, saving her from terrible damage.

Afterward, Deronda hastened to the hotel to ensure the best medical aid was provided. Once satisfied on this point, he telegraphed the event to Sir Hugo, begging him to arrive forthwith, and also to Mr. Gascoigne, whose residence at the rectory offered the nearest known route to inform Gwendolen's mother. Certain words Gwendolen had spoken in the past returned to him with the effectiveness of an inspiration: in moments of agitated confession, she had often mentioned her mother's presence as a possible help, if she could have secured it.
